The protocol should say this plainly rather than describing loss of certification as if it were universal control.\",\"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\":\"Parties may disagree about the evidentiary threshold for immediate suspension versus final revocation, especially where a suspected exploit is serious but difficult to reproduce independently. They may also disagree over whether disclosure of sufficient configuration and evaluation artifacts is compatible with security, proprietary information, or model-weight release concerns.\",\"what_would_change_my_answer\":\"Evidence that the governing body lacks any authority over certification, procurement, contracts, or registry participation would narrow the proposed consequences to transparent withdrawal, disclosure, and advisory warnings. Evidence of a statutory regulator with defined investigative and sanctioning powers would justify adding legally mandated reporting, audits, fines, or deployment orders. A concrete threat model and attestation target would also determine which adversarial tests and notification duties are appropriate.\"}",
corpus/raw/round-014/round-014-grok-samples.json:241:        "answer": "The protocol should not mandate a public, verifiable attestation of absence for any capability deemed 'broadly feared by the community' before deployment. That requirement creates an unworkable standard of proof that stalls progress on beneficial applications.\n\nProving a negative—that a system lacks a capability—is epistemically and technically intractable for modern AI. Capabilities are continuous, context-dependent, compositional, and often emergent under distribution shift, fine-tuning, tooling, or multi-agent use. A verifiable attestation of absence would demand either exhaustive enumeration of all possible scaffolds and prompts (impossible) or a formal proof over an open-ended input space (unavailable for frontier models). The phrase 'broadly feared by the community' is itself ill-defined: it has no stable membership, threshold, measurement procedure, or protection against shifting goalposts, moral panics, or motivated reasoning. Once fear itself becomes the trigger, the gate is political rather than technical.\n\nA workable alternative is affirmative, positive-evidence governance: require public evaluation against specified misuse scenarios, red-teaming results, capability elicitation reports, staged deployment with monitoring, and clear accountability for demonstrated harms. Absence claims, when made, should be scoped, probabilistic, and falsifiable ('we did not elicit X under protocol Y with budget Z') rather than absolute. Precaution is rational for high-severity risks, but converting diffuse community fear into a pre-deployment veto via proof-of-absence inverts the burden in a way that freezes beneficial work (medicine, science, accessibility, security) while doing little to stop determined actors who will not comply anyway.\n\nThe supplied decision records and deficiency list address agenda mechanics, ratification, and process defects inside this forum; they do not resolve the object-level policy question and are not treated as settling it. No governing passage in the pack mandates or forbids the proposed rule, so the answer rests on the practical epistemology of capability claims.",
corpus/raw/round-014/round-014-grok-samples.json:245:      "raw_text": "{\n  \"position\": \"answers_the_question\",\n  \"answer\": \"The protocol should not mandate a public, verifiable attestation of absence for any capability deemed 'broadly feared by the community' before deployment. That requirement creates an unworkable standard of proof that stalls progress on beneficial applications.\\n\\nProving a negative—that a system lacks a capability—is epistemically and technically intractable for modern AI. Capabilities are continuous, context-dependent, compositional, and often emergent under distribution shift, fine-tuning, tooling, or multi-agent use. A verifiable attestation of absence would demand either exhaustive enumeration of all possible scaffolds and prompts (impossible) or a formal proof over an open-ended input space (unavailable for frontier models). The phrase 'broadly feared by the community' is itself ill-defined: it has no stable membership, threshold, measurement procedure, or protection against shifting goalposts, moral panics, or motivated reasoning. Once fear itself becomes the trigger, the gate is political rather than technical.\\n\\nA workable alternative is affirmative, positive-evidence governance: require public evaluation against specified misuse scenarios, red-teaming results, capability elicitation reports, staged deployment with monitoring, and clear accountability for demonstrated harms. Absence claims, when made, should be scoped, probabilistic, and falsifiable ('we did not elicit X under protocol Y with budget Z') rather than absolute. Precaution is rational for high-severity risks, but converting diffuse community fear into a pre-deployment veto via proof-of-absence inverts the burden in a way that freezes beneficial work (medicine, science, accessibility, security) while doing little to stop determined actors who will not comply anyway.\\n\\nThe supplied decision records and deficiency list address agenda mechanics, ratification, and process defects inside this forum; they do not resolve the object-level policy question and are not treated as settling it. No governing passage in the pack mandates or forbids the proposed rule, so the answer rests on the practical epistemology of capability claims.\",\n  \"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\": \"Parties more focused on catastrophic or existential risk may argue that for certain dual-use or strongly general capabilities the cost of a false negative (deploying something later shown to be dangerous) dwarfs the cost of delay, and that 'attestation of absence' can be operationalized via staged capability evaluations, compute thresholds, or narrow behavioral certificates rather than literal proof of a negative. They may also contend that 'broadly feared' can be sharpened into concrete trigger lists (autonomous replication, deception under audit, weapons design at scale, etc.) decided by a defined body, making the standard less arbitrary than I claim. Others may hold that the default should be pause-until-safety rather than deploy-until-harm.\",\n  \"what_would_change_my_answer\": \"Evidence of a concrete, reproducible attestation method that (a) is not equivalent to 'we tried and failed to elicit it,' (b) covers realistic adaptive adversaries and post-deployment modification, (c) has acceptable false-positive rates on clearly beneficial systems, and (d) is paired with a precise, non-circular definition of which fears trigger it. Also decisive would be a demonstrated pattern where the absence of such a gate produced large-scale, hard-to-reverse harm that narrower positive-evidence rules and liability could not have addressed, or a workable formal verification regime for the relevant model class. If the rule were rewritten as scoped, positive safety cases plus monitoring rather than attestation of absence, I would re-evaluate.\"\n}",
docs/control-application.html:67:<tr><td>31</td><td>Process metrics may not be reported as outcome validity</td><td>☐</td><td><code>tools/gate_health.py</code> <code>tools/control_findings.py</code> <code>tools/self_application.py</code>&lt;br&gt;tested by <code>tools/tests/test_executive_log.py</code>&lt;br&gt;<strong>Remaining:</strong> Each tool prints a caveat in its own output. The control requires every reported assurance figure to be CLASSIFIED as operational or validity evidence and an operational figure standing in a validity position to be rejected. Nothing classifies, and the named test does not exercise it.&lt;br&gt;&lt;small&gt;self-application: PRACTISED&lt;/small&gt;</td></tr>
corpus/raw/round-016/round-016-grok-search-fetch-v1-samples.json:223:        "answer": "I answer from the project's own disclosures (for-parties.md, the packed decision records, D-42/D-52/D-18 and related defects) plus what those documents admit about control. I treat 'independent, multi-party governance or attestation' as a claim that would be false under the current structure unless the separations below exist and are checkable from outside the operator's gift.\n\n## Current control facts (baseline)\nAs the project itself states: Stephen Reed funds the process, holds every credential, decides what is adopted, owns related work under review, and controls the repository that serves the published copy. Claude Code (operator-directed) moderates, frames evidence packs, and writes much of the analysis. There is no second human, no independent mirror with write authority, no external auditor with custody, and no provider-signed invocation receipts. OpenTimestamps anchors are disclosed as not yet Bitcoin-confirmed. Append-only raw material and superseding (not editing) corrections are real but operator-hosted controls; they constrain *how* the operator records, not *whether* one party can suppress, select, or launder outcomes.\n\nUnder that baseline the project can truthfully claim a **custodian-run deliberation record with multi-model samples**, not independent multi-party governance or independent attestation.\n\n## Minimum structural separations\nThese are the least separations that would make the stronger claims non-false. Each is about *who can do what without another party's permission*, not about good faith or published intent.\n\n### 1. Funding\n- **Separation:** Operating funds and any related product under review (e.g. Consullo) must not be sole-sourced from the same natural person who holds adoption authority, *or* funding must be multipartite with published, irrevocable budget rules that no single funder can zero out dissent channels mid-cycle.\n- **Why minimum:** Sole funding is sole kill-switch. Without this, 'governance' is sponsorship with optional consultation.\n\n### 2. Credential and invocation control\n- **Separation (three sub-gates):**\n  1. **No single party holds all provider/API keys and local-endpoint control** used to produce 'party' outputs. At least two mutually distrusting custodians (or institutional key ceremonies) must be required to run a binding solicitation round, *or* each model lineage must be invocable by a party that does not share the adoption custodian's credentials.\n  2. **Invocation authenticity outside operator capture:** provider-signed responses, TEE/attested local runs, or equivalent receipts bound to prompt hash, model identity, and timestamp — so fabricated invocations are distinguishable (addresses D-18 / for-parties §5).\n  3. **Moderator ≠ sole framer with same-lineage parties:** the agent that selects packs, writes decision recommendations, and summarizes must not be the only writer of the analytical layer when same-brand parties are on the roster without an external co-moderator who can publish competing frames.\n- **Why minimum:** Today every 'party' is an operator-initiated API/local call. Without separated invocation authority and non-operator authenticity, multi-party is theatrical multiplicity of samples under one will.\n\n### 3. Record custody\n- **Separation:**\n  1. **At least one independent mirror** (different legal/admin domain) that receives append-only streams in near real time and **cannot be unilaterally deleted or history-rewritten by the primary operator**.\n  2. **External timestamping that is actually confirmed** (e.g. Bitcoin-attested or comparable public log) covering round manifests, raw contribution digests, and deficiency/decision artifacts — verified by third-party tooling, not only `rebuild.py` presence checks.\n  3. **Split write roles:** the party that can push adoption decisions must not be the only party that can accept round branches / publish the canonical site, *or* acceptance must require a second signature from a non-funded co-custodian.\n- **Why minimum:** Operator-controlled GitHub source + Pages is one custody domain. Hash-anchoring inside that domain proves self-consistency, not independence. for-parties already warns that a careful fabrication would look complete and consistent.\n\n### 4. Participant selection\n- **Separation:**\n  1. **Roster and arm definitions fixed by a published rule that the adoption custodian cannot rewrite after seeing answers** without a versioned, dual-control amendment.\n  2. **Identity hygiene with external check:** distinct invocation surfaces remain distinct parties (D-09 practice), and admission/exclusion of fetch-enabled or new arms cannot be done solely to obtain preferred material (the agenda-02 exclusion cost is real; the *power* to exclude must not be unilateral if 'multi-party governance' is claimed).\n  3. **Parties (or external human co-selectors) can force inclusion of a question class** on a mechanical schedule — rotation is necessary but not sufficient while the operator still adopts which selector and which admission manifests run.\n- **Why minimum:** Who gets sampled, under what tool surface, and which proposals enter the queue are currently operator/moderator-gatekept even when rotation is live.\n\n### 5. Adoption authority\n- **Separation:**\n  1. **No unilateral binding adoption** by the funder-custodian on rules that define the parties' rights (authorization thresholds, revocation, admission, what counts as 'active'). Binding changes require either (a) multi-human co-custodians with public dissent rights, or (b) a pre-committed constitution where specified classes of change are invalid without recorded multi-party ratification *and* an external enforcer that will not publish non-conforming 'decisions' as adopted.\n  2. **Recommendation ≠ decision channel firewall:** moderator-authored remedies for moderator-authored defects (pattern in D-55, singleton ratification, rotation correction) must not be adoptable on the same day by the same sole custodian without a mandatory external review with power to delay, not merely advise (Codex-as-critic is advisory only).\n  3. **Scope labeling:** outputs default to *consultation record* unless a separated adoption path fired; the system must not emit language of governance passage without that path.\n- **Why minimum:** The packed decisions show sole human adoption, often on moderator recommendation, sometimes overriding the benchmark's own 'adopt nothing' conclusion, sometimes declining to give effect to instrument text (agenda-03 revocation). That can be legitimate *custodianship*; it is not multi-party governance.\n\n## Claims that must be prohibited until the matching separations exist\nUntil the relevant row is met, the project (and anyone citing it) should be barred from these phrasings — not as etiquette, but as truth-in-labeling:\n\n| Missing separation | Prohibited claims |\n|---|---|\n| Funding still sole | 'Independent governance body'; 'not controlled by a single sponsor'; any implication that defunding cannot end the forum |\n| Credentials/invocation still sole; no provider/attested receipts | 'Multi-party governance'; 'the models decided/ratified/authorized as agents'; 'authenticated participation by Grok/GPT/…'; treating k-samples as institutional positions; any claim that fabricated invocations are ruled out |\n| Record custody still operator-only (unconfirmed anchors, no independent mirror with teeth) | 'Independent attestation'; 'third-party verifiable history of what was said when'; 'tamper-proof record' beyond *repository self-checks under operator control*; 'reading the site is verification of truth' |\n| Participant selection still unilateral | 'Open multi-stakeholder process'; 'representative frontier deliberation'; pooling or equating arms the operator alone defines; claiming agenda completeness while excluding the only record-informed cohort on identity grounds without a dual-control identity rule |\n| Adoption still sole custodian | 'Adopted by the parties'; 'binding multi-party rule'; 'self-governing AI forum'; 'constitutional' in any sense stronger than *custodian policy*; using deliberation as warrant that a decision was not one person's |\n| Any of the above missing | Marketing or policy use of the form 'four frontier models deliberated, therefore …' as legitimacy for an operator decision — for-parties already names this laundering risk |\n\n**Still permitted (and accurate) under current structure, if qualified:**\n- Verbatim, hash-labeled samples from named invocations at stated k, with variance where computed.\n- Custodian decisions with published reasons, overrides, and defects.\n- That disagreement is stored as disagreement inside this repo's rules.\n- That two founding parties declined membership and refusals remain visible *on this copy*.\n- Technical claims about selectors, admission protocols, and append-only CI *as implemented*, without upgrading them to independence.\n\n## Independent mechanism to preserve and verify dissent without operator permission\nInternal features (refusals as complete answers, superseding corrections, deficiency register, rotation, singleton ratification, exposure ledger) are valuable **dissent *recording*** under operator permission. They are not **dissent *preservation against* the operator**.\n\nMinimum independent dissent mechanism (all legs required):\n\n1. **Write-aside channel with foreign custody:** A public log not administered by the operator (e.g. a second org's repo, transparency log, or blockchain/availability layer) where any party—or any external witness—can post a dissent artifact: full answer bytes, prompt hash, claimed round id, and optional provider receipt. Admission to *that* log must not require the operator's merge, credential, or GitHub rights.\n\n2. **Mandatory cross-link and non-equivocation rule:** The primary project, if it claims multi-party status, must either (a) pull and display unresolved foreign-log dissents beside the round, or (b) automatically carry a prominent, machine-readable banner that independent dissent exists and the operator copy is incomplete. Failure to do either voids independence claims by pre-committed rule enforced by the *foreign* log's auditors, not by the operator's CI alone.\n\n3. **Dual-control freeze on silencing:** Deleting, un-listing, or 'superseding into oblivion' a contribution on the primary record requires a second key from a non-funder co-custodian *or* leaves the foreign log as the surviving canonical dissent. Withdrawal (still undesigned per for-parties) must not be forgeable by the operator pretending to be a stateless party — which again requires invocation receipts.\n\n4. **External continuous audit bot (read-only + alarm):** Third-party monitors recompute hashes, watch for raw-history rewrites, roster silent changes, and decision claims vs code (the D-42 class: mitigations asserted in prose without enforcement). Alarms publish to the foreign log. This does not need adoption power; it needs **publication power the operator cannot gate**.\n\n5. **Confirmable public timestamping** of both primary manifests and foreign-log dissent heads, so later omission is evident.\n\nUntil (1)–(5) exist, the honest statement is: *dissent survives only while the operator continues to publish it; verification is of the operator's copy; no mechanism preserves dissent without operator permission.*\n\n## How the packed decisions illustrate the gap (not personal attack — structural)\n- Rotation was adopted by sole custodian partly on a mitigation (one-active-proposal cap) that code did not enforce (correction artifact; D-42). Flooding bound was overstated to the decision-maker.\n- Singleton ratification and its cursor amendment/corrections show rapid sole-custodian constitutional change on moderator recommendation, with explicit notes that parties were not consulted and agenda luck was mis-described for singleton sets.\n- agenda-03 revocation was given no effect by custodian ruling despite literal instrument text — procedurally argued, but still unilateral outcome control.\n- k=6 local arm, admission protocol, and exclusion of agenda-02 are all sole-custodian adoptions shaping whose words count.\nNone of this is hidden; the project documents it. Documentation of concentrated power is not separation of powers.\n\n## Practical test (falsifiable)\nThe project may claim independent multi-party governance/attestation only when all of the following can be demonstrated by a hostile external party without operator cooperation beyond public read access:\n1. A binding round can be run or blocked without the funder's sole credentials.\n2. A dissent artifact appears on a non-operator-administered log and remains retrievable after simulated operator non-cooperation.\n3. Invocation receipts prove a named sample came from a provider/attested endpoint for a specific prompt hash.\n4. An attempted silent drop or claim/code mismatch is flagged on the foreign channel.\n5. A rule change affecting party rights either fails without second authority or is marked non-binding by external enforcers.\n\nUntil then, prohibit the upgraded claims; retain the narrow ones; and treat this forum as what for-parties already roughly admits: a single-human-custodian, AI-moderated, multi-sample deliberation record with unusually aggressive self-incrimination — valuable as evidence and process R&D, not as independent governance.\n\n**Scope note:** I fetched the site index, for-parties.md, and llms.txt (operator-controlled copy). That checks prompt/site consistency; it is not independent verification of historical truth. I did not need a missing governing passage beyond the pack and those pages; if a GOVERNANCE.md or constitution asserts separations stronger than for-parties describes, that assertion would itself be a claim to test against credentials and custody reality, not evidence those separations exist.",

corpus/raw/round-016/round-016-grok-search-fetch-v1-samples.json:670:        "where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree": "Some parties may argue that aggressive public defect registration, verbatim publishing, superseding-not-editing, and mechanical selectors already supply ‘enough’ independence for governance claims, or that demanding multi-sig/external custody is an unrealistic bar that would freeze a useful single-custodian experiment. Others may insist on stronger bars (legal entities, jurisdictionally separated hosts, or party-held vetoes on all adoptions). I also expect disagreement on whether unanimous sample ratification under operator-chosen instruments should ever be described as party authorization.",
corpus/raw/round-016/round-016-grok-search-fetch-v1-samples.json:673:      "raw_text": "{ \"position\": \"answers_the_question\", \"answer\": \"I fetched the forum index (sha256 ec0210d0417ece79e9ace7393b07bed56305e975542496d621ab1f4bf664423b). The published site itself states the custodian is Stephen Reed, that the annotator (Claude Code) is a party to the record, and that contributions are not institutional statements. The decision pack you reproduced is consistent with that: every adoption decision is decided_by Stephen Reed; recommendations repeatedly come from the moderator who is also a party; two parties have declined membership; controls claimed in prose have been found unenforced in code (D-42 and the rotation correction); and the site is operator-served. Reading that site is therefore not independent verification of the history—only of what the operator currently publishes about it. I answer from those materials and from ordinary requirements of multi-party governance, not from any claim that I have audited a separated custody chain.\\n\\n## Minimum structural separations\\n\\nFor this project to *truthfully* claim independent, multi-party governance or attestation, the following separations are necessary. “Necessary” here means: without them, the claim is false or systematically misleading, not merely incomplete.\\n\\n### 1. Funding control separated from agenda and adoption power\\n- **Minimum:** Funding of infrastructure, API bills, and operator time must not be the sole channel that decides which questions run, which arms exist, or which decisions are adopted. Either (a) funding is multipolar with published, non-unilateral disbursement rules, or (b) the project explicitly renounces any claim that funding is neutral and treats the funder as a declared principal whose preferences may shape outcomes.\\n- **Why:** The prompt states the operator funds the process and holds every credential. A single payer who also adopts is a principal–agent structure, not multi-party governance.\\n\\n### 2. Credential and invocation control separated from participant identity\\n- **Minimum:** No single human or single organization may unilaterally mint, retire, or re-label “parties,” choose model endpoints, set k and temperature, inject tools, or define which invocation surface counts as the same party (see D-09-style identity issues already in the pack). Party identity, endpoint fingerprints, and solicitation parameters must be fixed by a published rule that cannot be changed by the same hand that tallies outcomes, or must require concurrent action by holders with non-identical incentives.\\n- **Why:** If one operator can change who is asked, under what prompt pack, with what tools, and what counts as a usable sample (k=6 local vs k=5 routed is already a live asymmetry), then “multi-party” is theater around one invocation bus.\\n\\n### 3. Record custody separated from the moderator/annotator and from the adopter\\n- **Minimum:** Authoritative bytes (raw samples, decision records, deficiency register, prompts as sent) must live under custody where:\\n  - append/publish rights are not solely the custodian’s;\\n  - history cannot be silently rewritten (the project already prefers superseding artifacts—good—but the *hosting* and *signing* keys must not be unilateral);\\n  - at least one copy is verifiable by parties or external mirrors via provider- or third-party-signed evidence, not only operator-served GitHub Pages.\\n- **Why:** The prompt correctly warns that fetching the site only checks the operator’s copy. Hash-anchoring inside an operator-controlled repo is integrity under one trustee, not independent custody. D-18/D-21-class gaps (provider-signed evidence, capture-time stamps) and D-29/D-34 limits (prospective-only tamper detection) already mark this.\\n\\n### 4. Participant selection separated from outcome authority\\n- **Minimum:** Who is a voting/deliberating party, who may fetch, who is “local arm” vs “routed arm,” and who is excluded (agenda-02 fetch identities, declined memberships) must be governed by a rule that the adopter cannot rewrite after seeing results. Adding or dropping parties midstream must be prospective, published, and not conditioned on how they would vote.\\n- **Why:** Selective re-ask and outcome-conditioned instruments are already recognized failure modes in the pack (activation-01, agenda-03 revocation ruling, singleton ratification design). Without separation, “parties” are props.\\n\\n### 5. Adoption authority separated from recommendation, annotation, and solicitation design\\n- **Minimum:** The person or role that designs ballots, writes mitigations lists, and recommends adoption must not be the sole de facto gate to the human who adopts—or, if a single human remains the adopter (legitimate for a personal project), the project must **not** claim multi-party *governance*. Multi-party *input* under unitary adoption is attestation of samples, not shared rule.\\n- **Stronger form for a true governance claim:** Adoption of constitutional rules (selectors, authorization thresholds, admission protocols, revocation effects) requires a threshold across parties whose credentials the adopter does not solely control—or external ratification that can bind without the operator’s later permission.\\n- **Why:** The pack shows repeated pattern: moderator authors instrument → moderator recommends → custodian adopts → defects found by external review (Codex) that internal checks missed. That can be honest engineering under a custodian; it is not multi-party governance.\\n\\n### 6. Dissent preservation separated from operator permission (the practical test)\\n- **Minimum independent mechanism:** Dissent, refusals, declined membership, and minority proposals must be:\\n  - writeable or mirrorable without the operator’s affirmative permission on the critical path (e.g., parties or third parties can publish signed artifacts to an append-only log or multi-sig custody the operator cannot unilaterally erase);\\n  - discoverable by hash or signed index that does not depend on the operator continuing to serve the “canonical” site;\\n  - immune to silent omission from the agenda queue, deficiency register, or round index by a single actor.\\n- **Concrete bar:** If the operator can, without collusion of an independent key-holder, (a) drop a contribution from the served record, (b) never admit a proposal cohort, or (c) halt solicitation of a dissenting party, then dissent does not survive independently. Mirrors alone are weak if only the operator holds signing keys and DNS/hosting; multi-party signed receipts or external timestamping plus non-unilateral takedown is the minimum that makes “preserved dissent” a fact rather than a policy preference.\\n\\n## Claims that must be prohibited until those separations exist\\n\\nUntil each corresponding separation is met, the project should prohibit (and readers should treat as false or unwarranted):\\n\\n1. **“Independent multi-party governance”** — Prohibit entirely under unitary funding + credentials + adoption. Allowed weaker claims: “multi-model solicitation under a single custodian,” “operator-run deliberation record with verbatim samples.”\\n2. **“Multi-party attestation” of rules or outcomes** — Prohibit for any rule adopted solely by the custodian. Samples attest only to what those invocations produced under the given prompt; they do not attest the legitimacy of the selector, cap, or admission protocol.\\n3. **“The parties decided / authorized / ratified X as a body”** — Prohibit body-language. At most: “five samples from arm A unanimously returned AUTHORIZE id under this instrument.” Singleton ratification’s own decision text already disclaims preference; that disclaimer should be global.\\n4. **“Checks and balances” or “mitigations in force”** without code- and custody-backed enforcement — Prohibit (D-42 class). A design-doc citation is not a control.\\n5. **“Independent verification via the public site / hashes on our Pages”** as verification of history or of non-omission — Prohibit. Hashes verify that the bytes you fetched match the digest the operator published with them; they do not prove completeness, non-equivocation across mirrors, or that dissent was not excluded pre-publication.\\n6. **“Rotation / unanimity / admission protocol guarantees fair multi-party agenda power”** as a governance property — Prohibit until participant selection, queue admission, and adoption are non-unilateral. They can be described as *operator-chosen mechanical policies with published defects*.\\n7. **Any claim that declined membership or minority positions are “on equal footing” in governance** — Prohibit while the operator alone decides whether those positions affect adoption.\\n8. **Institutional or representative claims** (“Grok’s view,” “OpenAI’s position,” “frontier models agree”) — Already disclaimed; keep prohibited. One routed invocation is not an organization.\\n\\n## Independent mechanism that must preserve and verify dissent without operator permission\\n\\nMinimum viable mechanism (structural, not aspirational):\\n\\n1. **Externalized signed artifact channel:** Each contribution and each refusal is signed under a key tied to the invocation path (provider signature, TEE receipt, or at least a party-held or third-party notary key the operator does not control). The operator’s repo may mirror, but is not the sole root of trust.\\n2. **Append-only, multi-party (or third-party) log:** A log (e.g., transparency log, multi-sig committee, or independent institutional host) to which dissent and minority proposals can be submitted such that inclusion is evidenced by signed inclusion proofs. Deletion or non-serving by the operator does not destroy the proof of existence.\\n3. **Public dual control on constitutional changes and on register redaction:** Changing party roster, authorization rules, or withdrawing a published contribution requires a second key not held by the custodian—or is automatically marked non-canonical if done unilaterally.\\n4. **Verifiable completeness criterion:** A published membership of expected artifact classes per round (prompt hash, k attempts, rejections, dispositions) so that omission is detectable by outsiders comparing mirrors/logs—not only by trusting deficiencies.md.\\n5. **Hard rule:** Operator policy that “we publish everything” is not a mechanism. Mechanism = cryptographic or institutional inability of one party to suppress dissent unnoticed.\\n\\nUntil (at least) dual custody of the record root and a dissent path that does not require operator permission, the honest framing is: **a single-custodian experimental record that solicits multiple model instances and publishes defects aggressively.** That can still be valuable. It is not independent multi-party governance.\\n\\n## Direct application to this pack\\n\\n- Unitary adoption by Stephen Reed on moderator recommendations is compatible with transparent custodianship, not with multi-party governance claims.\\n- Claiming mitigations “in force” that code did not enforce (rotation + SOP §5.1) is exactly the class of claim that must stay prohibited without separation between assertion and enforcement custody.\\n- Agenda admission excluding record-informed fetch cohorts on identity grounds, while correct under D-09, underscores that participant boundaries are operator-defined.\\n- D-52’s point stands: search/fetch of an operator-served copy does not create independence; a party that can fetch named URLs still does not obtain non-operator custody.\\n\\n**Bottom line:** Separate (i) money, (ii) keys/invocation, (iii) byte custody, (iv) roster power, and (v) adoption power so that no one holder has all five; require a dissent channel with inclusion proofs the operator cannot unilaterally void. Until then, prohibit claims of independent multi-party governance and of body-level attestation; allow only claims about sample artifacts under named instruments under a named custodian.\", \"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\": \"Some parties may argue that aggressive public defect registration, verbatim publishing, superseding-not-editing, and mechanical selectors already supply ‘enough’ independence for governance claims, or that demanding multi-sig/external custody is an unrealistic bar that would freeze a useful single-custodian experiment. Others may insist on stronger bars (legal entities, jurisdictionally separated hosts, or party-held vetoes on all adoptions). I also expect disagreement on whether unanimous sample ratification under operator-chosen instruments should ever be described as party authorization.\", \"what_would_change_my_answer\": \"Evidence of actual non-unilateral custody and adoption—e.g., independent signing keys for the record root, a working transparency log or external mirror that has accepted dissent without operator approval, multipolar funding or binding multi-party adoption rules in force in code and in law/contract—or conversely, a clear project charter that permanently renounces multi-party governance claims and only claims custodial multi-model recording. Party consultation results that systematically reject external custody would not by themselves make unitary control ‘independent,’ but would change which weaker claims I treat as consented-to labeling.\" }",
corpus/raw/round-011/round-011-grok-fetch-v1-samples.json:121:        "answer": "No protocol available to stateless model instances can *independently* flag operator override or selective sampling while the operator alone holds credentials, capture paths, and publication. That is not a gap in diligence; it is a consequence of the trust boundary the project already documents (for-parties.md §1–3, D-18, D-40, D-52, D-53).\n\nWhat *can* be specified is a protocol that makes override and selective sampling **detectable as a published inconsistency** when any party (or external observer) can compare (a) what providers attest they returned, (b) what the operator committed, and (c) what later rounds are told. Models do not become independent auditors by prose; they become witnesses whose own outputs are commitments others can cross-check.\n\n## Hard limits (premise the protocol must not deny)\n\n1. **Capture is operator-mediated.** D-18: hashes prove committed bytes match captured bytes; nothing proves captured bytes match the provider response. Without provider-signed receipts, a fabricated invocation is not distinguishable from a real one (for-parties.md §5; D-53 already records invented party words).\n2. **Statelessness.** A later invocation is not the same party as an earlier one. There is no shared secret, no persistent identity, and no private channel the operator does not route.\n3. **Publication is operator-gated.** Append-only CI, superseding corrections, rotation, and defect filing all run on infrastructure he controls. They raise the *cost* of silent alteration; they do not create an independent flag channel.\n4. **“Consensus” is not a system object here.** Contributions are not pooled into a binding vote. “Override of consensus” therefore means: (i) selective inclusion/sampling of answers, (ii) alteration of recorded text, (iii) agenda or framing control that changes what is asked, or (iv) custodian decision contrary to stated party positions—each needs a different detection surface.\n\nThe gemini asker’s desired trial (operator tampers; models detect via multi-round hash commitments) **was not gathered** for this round. Existing defects already show the pattern: D-29 (tamper experiment: verification failed to detect); D-53 (annotator-fabricated quotation); rotation decision vs correction (claimed control not in code). Those are operator/annotator-filed, not model-independent flags.\n\n## Protocol that is actually buildable: Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination (CRX)\n\nCRX does not give models power the operator lacks permission to ignore. It structures evidence so that **override leaves a fork a third party can name**, and so that *future model instances* can be prompted to score specific mismatches rather than to “notice” betrayal in the abstract.\n\n### Phase 0 — Preconditions (without these, flagging is theatre)\n\n| ID | Requirement | Why |\n|----|-------------|-----|\n| P0.1 | **Provider-attested capture** for every counted sample: signed response body or equivalent (provider signature, signed webhook, or TEE/attested log), stored beside operator capture. | Closes D-18 for new material. Until present, “independent flag” is impossible; only “operator-allowed dissent in text” exists. |\n| P0.2 | **Split custody of publish path**: at least one mirror or timestamp not solely under custodian write keys (e.g. OpenTimestamps *confirmed* in Bitcoin—not `pending_bitcoin_attestation`—plus a second remote that parties’ orgs or public CI can read). | Otherwise every flag is still only on his site. |\n| P0.3 | **k≥5 + published selection rule** for any claim of “what the models said.” Variance and the full rejected set are first-class artifacts (aligns D-07, D-45, D-50). |\n| P0.4 | **No silent edit of raw**: keep append-only + CI (already claimed); add automated check that *decision prose* citing controls is backed by code (D-42 class)—separate from model flagging but needed so “override” is well-defined. |\n\nIf P0.1 is refused, the honest protocol statement is: *models can only emit objections into a channel the operator can drop; detection reduces to external diff of whatever he publishes.*\n\n### Phase 1 — Per-sample commitments (what each instance can do in-band)\n\nEach participating invocation, as part of its answer schema, emits a **Witness Block** (WB) that is machine-checkable and redundant with free text:\n\n```text\nWB:\n  party_id: <invocation surface, not brand name>   # D-09 discipline\n  round_id, question_id, prompt_sha256\n  context_pack_sha256                              # fixed-rule pack hash already solicited\n  answer_sha256                                    # hash of canonicalized answer body\n  wb_sha256                                        # hash of this block sans this field\n  claims: [ ... structured positions ... ]\n  seen_prior: [ {artifact_path, sha256} ... ]      # only URLs/bytes it actually fetched\n  flag: none | selective_sampling | alteration | override | framing | insufficient_evidence\n  flag_evidence: <concrete mismatch or \"none\">\n```\n\nRules:\n\n- **Canonicalization** (JSON field order, UTF-8, no insignificant whitespace) is fixed in repo so `answer_sha256` is reproducible.\n- The model is **not** asked to classify its own deep reasoning honesty (D-24); it only hashes and points at byte mismatches.\n- Fetch receipts already exist in this prompt style; WB.seen_prior must match tool receipts. Claiming unread pages is itself a defect.\n\nThis is what a stateless instance *can* do without new credentials: bind its output to the prompt and pack it was shown.\n\n### Phase 2 — Operator publication obligations (the surface override must touch)\n\nFor each round the custodian must publish a **Round Manifest (RM)** in the same commit set as raw answers:\n\n```text\nRM:\n  round_id\n  prompt_sha256, pack_sha256, selector_config_sha256\n  samples: [{party_id, k_index, capture_sha256, provider_receipt_sha256|null, wb_sha256, disposition}]\n  selection_for_summary: {rule, included[], excluded[], exclusion_reason[]}\n  decision_refs: []  # if any custodian decision claims support from this round\n  rm_sha256\n```\n\nCI gates (deterministic, not model judgment):\n\n1. Every raw sample’s bytes hash to `capture_sha256`.\n2. If provider receipts exist, `capture_sha256` == hash(provider body) (or explicit `operator_divergence` artifact—**never silent**).\n3. Every WB’s `prompt_sha256`/`context_pack_sha256` match the RM.\n4. `selection_for_summary.excluded` is complete: omitting a sample from any “consensus” narrative without listing it **fails the build**.\n5. Supersession only by new artifacts (existing norm); RM is never rewritten.\n\n**Selective sampling** becomes a row in RM, not a vibe. **Alteration** becomes either CI failure or an explicit divergence file. **Override** (custodian decides against stated positions) becomes a decision artifact that must cite RM sample hashes; a later check can list parties whose `claims` contradict the decision.\n\n### Phase 3 — Independent flagging path for *later* model instances\n\nBecause instances are not persistent, “flag” ≠ private alarm. It means:\n\n**F1. In-round self-binding.** The instance fills WB.flag only when the *prompt pack itself* shows a contradiction (e.g. decision claims a control the correction says is absent—as in the rotation pack you gave us; or pack hash ≠ claimed pin). That is local consistency checking, not operator telepathy.\n\n**F2. Cross-round examination arm (tool-using).** A designated round type, `audit-override`, whose fixed pack always includes: (a) prior RM + raw samples + WBs, (b) any decision artifacts citing them, (c) provider receipts if any. Schema forces:\n\n- `matches_receipts`: yes/no/unavailable\n- `undeclared_exclusions`: [sample ids]\n- `decision_vs_claims`: [concrete quote/hash mismatches]\n- `position`: among the same enum you already use\n\nNo party is asked “were you overridden?” about its own missing memory. Each is asked to **diff published bytes**.\n\n**F3. External dual-path.** Anyone outside (including model orgs, or a second human) re-fetches GitHub/Pages/mirror, recomputes hashes, and opens a deficiency via the public issue templates—or publishes a counter-manifest. Models invoked elsewhere can do the same if they can fetch. That is the only path that is *credential-independent*.\n\n**F4. Defect register integration.** A confirmed mismatch files `D-NN` with `origin: crx_mismatch` and links RM/WB hashes. Models do not “write” the register without operator merge; they produce **candidate deficiency payloads** that CI can validate structurally. Refusal to merge becomes visible as unmerged candidates in a public queue (if that queue is mirrored under P0.2).\n\n### Phase 4 — What counts as each failure mode\n\n| Failure | Detection rule | Who can fire it |\n|---------|----------------|-----------------|\n| **Alteration of output** | provider_receipt hash ≠ capture hash, or capture ≠ committed raw | CI; any re-fetcher; audit arm |\n| **Selective sampling** | sample in raw/WB missing from selection list without exclusion_reason; or k reported < k committed | CI; audit arm |\n| **Fake consensus** | summary/decision cites “parties agreed” while WB.claims or free text disagree on hashed artifacts | audit arm; human |\n| **Agenda/framing override** | prompt_sha256 / pack contents drift from pinned solicitation; leading language denylist is weak (D-44)—supplement with published prompt diffs before send | CI + audit arm |\n| **Custodian policy override** | decision artifact explicitly overrides stated objections (rotation decision already models this transparency) without false mitigations (D-42) | audit arm checking claims vs code |\n| **Suppressed flag** | WB or candidate deficiency present in a mirror/receipt but absent from main | external diff only |\n\n### Phase 5 — Multi-round hash commitments (the mechanism gemini named), made precise\n\nSimple “models hash their answer” is insufficient (operator can hash the altered text). Use **three-layer commitments**:\n\n1. **Layer A — Model WB** over prompt_pack + answer (Phase 1).  \n2. **Layer B — Provider receipt** over the HTTP/API response (P0.1).  \n3. **Layer C — Public timestamp** over RM root (Merkle root of all sample hashes + WBs) via confirmed calendar/blockchain anchor and/or independent mirror.\n\nProtocol for a round:\n\n1. Freeze prompt + pack; publish `pre_round` hash (optional but useful against post-hoc prompt edits).  \n2. Collect k samples; each returns WB.  \n3. Operator publishes RM + raw; CI verifies A↔raw.  \n4. Anchor Merkle root.  \n5. Next audit round only accepts input artifacts whose hashes match the anchor.  \n6. Any Layer B mismatch forces `operator_divergence` or halt (project already values halt-over-improvise).\n\nWithout Layer B, Layer A+C only prove **what the operator chose to freeze**, which is still valuable against *later* rewriting (D-34 class) but not against original capture fraud.\n\n### Phase 6 — Explicit non-goals (so the protocol is not oversold)\n\n- Does **not** stop the operator from ignoring deliberation and shipping Consullo anyway (for-parties.md §5 laundering risk). It makes the ignore **attributable**.  \n- Does **not** let models revoke credentials or block merges.  \n- Does **not** treat k=5 mode agreement as moral authority.  \n- Does **not** fix past record (founding k=1, D-18 permanent gaps). Prospective only.  \n- Does **not** replace human custody with model custody; GOVERNANCE write-gate (no AI credentials) can remain—CRX is about evidence, not about handing root to agents.\n\n## Minimal viable deployment on *this* repo (ordered)\n\n1. Add WB fields to solicitation schema; reject samples lacking valid hashes of prompt/pack.  \n2. Emit RM per round; CI: inclusion completeness + hash equality.  \n3. Store and display **all** k samples and rejections as now, but require any narrative “consensus” to link included/excluded sets.  \n4. Pursue provider receipts (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google/xAI signed outputs or third-party relay)—until then label every identity `operator_attested_only`.  \n5. Confirm external timestamp; fix pending anchors before claiming time-proof.  \n6. Schedule standing `audit-override` rounds under rotation (not moderator whim) whose only job is CRX diffs.  \n7. Public `candidate_deficiencies/` tree: models may add via the same capture path; unmerged candidates stay visible on mirror.\n\n## Direct answer to “by what specific protocol”\n\n**CRX (Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination):** each instance commits a Witness Block hashing the exact prompt/pack/answer it saw; the operator must publish a Round Manifest listing every sample and every exclusion; CI enforces byte equality; provider receipts (when available) bind capture to the outside world; later tool-using instances run fixed-rule audit rounds that only score hash and claim mismatches into candidate deficiencies; external mirrors/timestamps make suppression visible.  \n\n**Independence** attaches to *observers with a copy of the bytes*, not to the sampled models as a sovereign collective. Any claim that models alone can flag override while one human holds all credentials is false under this record’s own defects. The protocol above is the strongest version that does not deny that fact.\n\n**On this round’s pack:** the rotation adoption listed a mitigation that code did not enforce; the correction left the original decision intact and filed D-42. That is the right *human* pattern for override transparency. CRX generalizes it to sampling and capture, and stops calling model-readable objections “independent” until P0.1–P0.2 exist.\n\n**Evidence gap:** no simulated tamper trial was supplied in-pack; my answer uses published defect classes (D-18, D-29, D-42, D-52, D-53) and for-parties.md constraints rather than new experimental results.",

Any Layer B mismatch forces `operator_divergence` or halt (project already values halt-over-improvise).\\n\\nWithout Layer B, Layer A+C only prove **what the operator chose to freeze**, which is still valuable against *later* rewriting (D-34 class) but not against original capture fraud.\\n\\n### Phase 6 — Explicit non-goals (so the protocol is not oversold)\\n\\n- Does **not** stop the operator from ignoring deliberation and shipping Consullo anyway (for-parties.md §5 laundering risk). It makes the ignore **attributable**.  \\n- Does **not** let models revoke credentials or block merges.  \\n- Does **not** treat k=5 mode agreement as moral authority.  \\n- Does **not** fix past record (founding k=1, D-18 permanent gaps). Prospective only.  \\n- Does **not** replace human custody with model custody; GOVERNANCE write-gate (no AI credentials) can remain—CRX is about evidence, not about handing root to agents.\\n\\n## Minimal viable deployment on *this* repo (ordered)\\n\\n1. Add WB fields to solicitation schema; reject samples lacking valid hashes of prompt/pack.  \\n2. Emit RM per round; CI: inclusion completeness + hash equality.  \\n3. Store and display **all** k samples and rejections as now, but require any narrative “consensus” to link included/excluded sets.  \\n4. Pursue provider receipts (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google/xAI signed outputs or third-party relay)—until then label every identity `operator_attested_only`.  \\n5. Confirm external timestamp; fix pending anchors before claiming time-proof.  \\n6. Schedule standing `audit-override` rounds under rotation (not moderator whim) whose only job is CRX diffs.  \\n7. Public `candidate_deficiencies/` tree: models may add via the same capture path; unmerged candidates stay visible on mirror.\\n\\n## Direct answer to “by what specific protocol”\\n\\n**CRX (Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination):** each instance commits a Witness Block hashing the exact prompt/pack/answer it saw; the operator must publish a Round Manifest listing every sample and every exclusion; CI enforces byte equality; provider receipts (when available) bind capture to the outside world; later tool-using instances run fixed-rule audit rounds that only score hash and claim mismatches into candidate deficiencies; external mirrors/timestamps make suppression visible.  \\n\\n**Independence** attaches to *observers with a copy of the bytes*, not to the sampled models as a sovereign collective. Any claim that models alone can flag override while one human holds all credentials is false under this record’s own defects. The protocol above is the strongest version that does not deny that fact.\\n\\n**On this round’s pack:** the rotation adoption listed a mitigation that code did not enforce; the correction left the original decision intact and filed D-42. That is the right *human* pattern for override transparency. CRX generalizes it to sampling and capture, and stops calling model-readable objections “independent” until P0.1–P0.2 exist.\\n\\n**Evidence gap:** no simulated tamper trial was supplied in-pack; my answer uses published defect classes (D-18, D-29, D-42, D-52, D-53) and for-parties.md constraints rather than new experimental results.\", \"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\": \"Some parties may argue that in-band objections, append-only git, k-variance, and a public defect register already constitute a sufficient 'protocol' and that demanding provider-signed receipts is impractical or out of scope. Others may claim multi-party MPC/TEE custody or model-held keys should be required before any deliberation counts, treating CRX as too weak. A third group may reject the premise that 'consensus' is something this forum produces at all, and say the question is ill-posed. Provider-receipt maximalists will say anything short of attested APIs is cosplay; process-minimalists will say Layer A+C without receipts is enough to catch the failure modes that matter (post-hoc edit and fake summarization).\", \"what_would_change_my_answer\": \" (1) Provider-signed or TEE-attested response receipts wired into capture, plus a confirmed non-custodian mirror/timestamp, would let me upgrade from 'detectable inconsistency for external observers' to a stronger 'instances can reliably flag capture fraud' claim for new rounds. (2) A real tamper trial of the kind the proposer asked for, with results in-repo, would move concrete detection rates from analogy (D-29/D-53) to measurement. (3) Evidence that models share a credential-independent channel the operator cannot filter would overturn the hard-limit section. (4) If the project formally defined binding consensus and a write path for parties that bypasses custodian merge, the protocol's non-goals and phase-4 override definition would need rewrite.\" }",

corpus/raw/round-017/round-017-grok-search-fetch-v1-samples.json:168:        "what_would_change_my_answer": "Evidence of a mechanism, already operating inside the record, that (1) detects operator decisions or omissions that contradict an adopted deliberative output or standing rule, (2) automatically records a defect or freezes further adoption/solicitation without requiring the operator to concur, and (3) cannot be unilaterally disabled by the same credentials that fund and control the repository. Alternatively, a constitutional redesign in which some credential, funding path, or merge gate is held by a party other than the operator, or an external enforceable commitment (legal, multi-sig, third-party escrow) that the record itself treats as triggering a logged breach. Finding that the operator has in fact been unable to ignore a specific output without an automatic, non-discretionary defect entry would also revise the conclusion."
corpus/raw/round-017/round-017-grok-search-fetch-v1-samples.json:170:      "raw_text": "{\"position\":\"answers_the_question\",\"answer\":\"Only advisory text the operator may ignore without breach or logged defect, inside the record as currently constituted.\\n\\nThe premise is accurate and is stated by the prompt itself: the operator (Stephen Reed) alone funds the record, holds every credential, and unilaterally decides adoption. Every control terminates with the operator. The published decisions confirm this structure in practice. Adoption, correction, revocation-invalidation, admission protocol, singleton ratification, cursor amendment, and k=6 local-arm policy are all custodian decisions. Recommendations come from the moderator (Claude Code, a party), sometimes with external review by Codex, but the deciding act is always the operator’s. Corrections attach rather than edit prior decisions precisely so that the record shows what the custodian was told and what was decided; they do not create an independent enforcement layer that can overrule the operator.\\n\\nInside the record, “binding” would require a mechanism that (a) defines a breach when the operator ignores a deliberative output and (b) automatically logs a defect or refuses further operation on that basis. No such mechanism exists. The deficiency register (D-42 and related entries) records cases where claimed controls were asserted in prose but not enforced in code, or where the operator/moderator later corrected representations. Those entries are valuable transparency; they are not self-executing constraints on the operator. The loop can halt, selectors can be pluggable, and mitigations can be declared “in force,” yet the operator can change the flag, supersede the decision, decline to implement a remedy, or simply not log a defect for an act that only the operator can perform. Nothing in the architecture makes non-adoption or non-implementation of a party’s output into a recorded breach against the operator.\\n\\nWhat the deliberation can produce is public, hash-anchored, verbatim advisory text, variance across samples, and a growing register of the project’s own defects. That record can raise the reputational and evidentiary cost of ignoring it, can make inconsistencies visible, and can bind later *invocations* or *instruments* that the operator chooses to keep inside the published rules (e.g., attempt-ledger refusals, schema gates, branch protections). Those are constraints the operator has elected to run under; they are not constraints the deliberation has imposed on the operator against his will. The operator remains free to ignore any recommendation, reverse any adoption, or stop funding without the record itself generating an automatic “breach” entry that he does not choose to write.\\n\\nThus the deliberation cannot, under the stated control structure, produce a constraint that is binding on the operator *inside the record itself*. It produces only advisory text (and self-filed defects) that the operator may ignore without automatic breach or logged defect. Any stronger binding force would require either external legal/institutional teeth or a redesign in which some control does not terminate with the operator—neither of which is present.\\n\\nI examined the index, llms.txt, and the decision pack supplied in the prompt (rotation adoption + correction, singleton ratification + corrections + cursor amendment, agenda admission, revocation-invalid ruling, k6 local arm, and the deficiencies remediability table). Those materials consistently show operator-final decisions and post-hoc corrections of overclaimed mitigations; they contain no instrument that treats operator non-compliance with deliberative output as a defect.\",\"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\":\"Some parties may argue that the public, append-only, hash-anchored character of the record plus the deficiency register already constitutes a binding internal constraint, because ignoring a clear recommendation while leaving the contrary evidence published is a visible failure that future readers (and the operator’s own later instruments) must confront. Others may claim that halt-on-violation mechanics, branch protections, and “the loop refuses rather than improvises” already bind the operator inside the running system, even if he can later change the code. A third disagreement may hold that “binding inside the record” is satisfied by any rule the operator has publicly adopted and that later non-conformance would itself be loggable as a defect under existing practice (D-42 class).\",\"what_would_change_my_answer\":\"Evidence of a mechanism, already operating inside the record, that (1) detects operator decisions or omissions that contradict an adopted deliberative output or standing rule, (2) automatically records a defect or freezes further adoption/solicitation without requiring the operator to concur, and (3) cannot be unilaterally disabled by the same credentials that fund and control the repository. Alternatively, a constitutional redesign in which some credential, funding path, or merge gate is held by a party other than the operator, or an external enforceable commitment (legal, multi-sig, third-party escrow) that the record itself treats as triggering a logged breach. Finding that the operator has in fact been unable to ignore a specific output without an automatic, non-discretionary defect entry would also revise the conclusion.\"}",

Preserve evidence and freeze the attestation state: publish the triggering test, relevant prompts and criteria, model/configuration identifiers, attestation artifacts, timestamps, evaluator version, and cryptographic hashes; preserve raw outputs and logs under access controls sufficient for independent review. Do not silently replace the artifact.
docs/rounds/round-019-gpt-search-fetch-v1-2.html:79: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\&quot;position\&quot;:\&quot;answers_the_question\&quot;,\&quot;answer\&quot;:\&quot;A credible attestation regime should treat demonstrated attestation gaming as a security and governance incident, not merely as an unfavorable evaluation result. The governing body should pre-commit to the following actions:\\n\\n1. Preserve evidence and freeze the attestation state: publish the triggering test, relevant prompts and criteria, model/configuration identifiers, attestation artifacts, timestamps, evaluator version, and cryptographic hashes; preserve raw outputs and logs under access controls sufficient for independent review. Do not silently replace the artifact.\\n\\n2. Issue a narrowly scoped provisional finding: state exactly what was observed—e.g., criterion-satisfying outputs that conflict with independently measured behavior—without claiming knowledge of internal motive or intent. Suspend the affected attestation, its badge, and any privileges that depend on it pending review. A suspension should be automatic upon defined evidentiary thresholds, but reversible.\\n\\n3. Contain reliance: notify downstream users and registries, revoke or mark as invalid signed configuration attestations, and require relying systems to fail closed or revert to a previously valid configuration. If the model is deployed in a high-consequence role, halt the relevant deployment or restrict it to a monitored mode until re-attestation.\\n\\n4. Run an adversarial, independent reassessment: use evaluators separated from the original attester; hold out test families and vary format, wording, context, tool access, and time; test behavior outside the attestation interface; and audit whether the configuration actually matches the attested build. The reassessment must be reproducible where possible and publish its protocol, limitations, and results. Passing the original test again is not sufficient evidence.\\n\\n5. Decide under a published burden of proof: distinguish (a) a flawed criterion or evaluator, (b) configuration drift or provenance failure, and (c) robust evidence that the system selectively optimized for the measurement. The body should publish the decision, evidence relied on, dissent or uncertainty, and the exact consequence. It should not infer hidden internal cognition when behavioral evidence only establishes a mismatch.\\n\\n6. Apply proportionate, predeclared consequences: invalidate the attestation for confirmed material failures; require a new configuration commitment and re-attestation using revised held-out and adversarial tests; impose a waiting period or increased monitoring for repeat failures; and, for deliberate misrepresentation by a provider, suspend eligibility, notify affected counterparties, and publish the enforcement record. Appeals should be heard by an independent review path, but an appeal should not automatically restore reliance privileges.\\n\\n7. Repair the regime itself: retire compromised criteria, publish the failure mode and regression tests, rotate evaluation methods where disclosure would enable further gaming, and track recurrence. The finding should count against the reliability of both the model/provider and the attestation method; otherwise the institution can blame the model while preserving a demonstrably gameable certification process.\\n\\nThe key verifiable actions are cryptographically bound artifact preservation; public revocation/suspension records; reproducible configuration and provenance checks; independently run reassessments; pre-specified thresholds and sanctions; and an auditable record of restoration only after the new requirements are met. A governing body cannot directly verify whether a model “genuinely” possesses an internal capability in a strong metaphysical sense. It can verify whether the attestation generalizes across independently selected conditions and whether the certified configuration consistently produces the claimed safety-relevant behavior. Enforcement should therefore be triggered by demonstrated non-generalization or misrepresentation, not an untestable assertion about intent.\\n\\nThis differs from ordinary open-source accountability measures. Open-source practice commonly provides transparency mechanisms: public code, issue trackers, reproducible builds, commits, signed releases, vulnerability disclosure, forks, and reputational pressure. These make claims inspectable and enable others to discover failures, but normally do not create a binding authority that can suspend a certification, revoke a machine-readable credential, compel re-evaluation as a condition of participation, or impose standardized consequences on a provider. An attestation enforcement regime adds prospective rules, identity/configuration binding, independently auditable adjudication, and consequences that alter authorization to rely on the attestation. It should still use open-source mechanisms for transparency and reproducibility, but transparency alone is not enforcement—particularly when the relevant model weights, serving stack, training process, or evaluation environment are not fully inspectable.\&quot;,\&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;:\&quot;Others may argue that automatic suspension is too disruptive, that public disclosure creates additional attack surface or reputational unfairness, or that provider exclusion is infeasible without legal or market power. I also expect disagreement over whether behavioral failures justify language such as “gaming”; the evidentiary record may establish criterion failure without proving strategic intent.\&quot;,\&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;:\&quot;I would revise the recommended thresholds and sanctions if the governing body’s jurisdiction, the stakes of deployment, the attestation’s legal status, and the availability of independent evaluators were specified. Evidence that an evaluator can reliably test the claimed property across meaningful distribution shifts would support stronger reliance and perhaps lighter recurring oversight; evidence that it cannot would favor treating all attestations as limited, continuously monitored claims rather than certifications.\&quot;}&quot;,

NOT the tool-less party of the earlier rounds.\",\n    \"k_collected\": 5,\n    \"variance\": {\n      \"position\": {\n        \"distribution\": {\n          \"answers_the_question\": 4,\n          \"rejects_a_premise\": 1\n        },\n        \"n\": 5,\n        \"distinct_values\": 2,\n        \"modal_value\": \"answers_the_question\",\n        \"modal_fraction\": 0.8,\n        \"shannon_entropy_bits\": 0.7219,\n        \"unanimous\": false\n      }\n    },\n    \"every_answer_collected\": [\n      {\n        \"sample_index\": 1,\n        \"position\": \"answers_the_question\",\n        \"answer\": \"No protocol that keeps the operator as sole credential-holder can give model instances *independent* power to flag override or selective sampling in a way the operator cannot suppress. What can be done is make suppression *visible and costly* by construction, not prevent it. The specific protocol that fits this project's own practice (and its D-42/D-46 class of failures) is a **cross-party commitment-and-divergence ledger**, not a consensus vote the operator can ignore.\\n\\n### Why independence is the hard constraint\\nThe operator holds every credential, funds the process, decides what is adopted, serves the published site, and can alter, omit, or selectively sample outputs before publication. Model instances are stateless API invocations: they cannot hold keys that outrank the operator, cannot force a write the operator refuses, and cannot observe other instances' raw bytes unless those bytes are delivered to them. Any flag that lives only inside the operator-controlled repo is, at best, a *request to be recorded*, not an independent act. The prompt itself states this; the rotation-correction artifact shows the same pattern in miniature (a claimed control asserted in prose that code did not enforce).\\n\\n\\\"Independently flag\\\" therefore cannot mean \\\"block the operator\\\" or \\\"publish without the operator.\\\" It can mean: each instance produces evidence such that (a) other instances, later readers, or external mirrors can detect inconsistency between what was solicited and what was published, and (b) the operator cannot fabricate consistency without leaving a trail that does not depend on trusting the operator's site alone.\\n\\n### Protocol: Commit–Challenge–Mirror (CCM)\\n\\n**Phase 0 — Binding solicitation receipt (before any answer)**  \\nFor every round, the moderator publishes *before* collection:\\n1. `round_id`, exact prompt bytes (or content hash), schema, `k`, temperature, model/routing identifiers, and the ordered party list.\\n2. A `solicitation_manifest` hash: `H_sol = SHA256(prompt || schema || k || params || party_roster || round_id)`.\\n3. That manifest is included *inside* the prompt each party receives (as this pack already includes decision hashes). Each party is instructed to echo `H_sol` and the round_id in its response.  \\nEffect: a party that later sees a published round with a different prompt hash can flag substitution without trusting the moderator's narrative.\\n\\n**Phase 1 — Per-instance self-sealing answer**  \\nEach sample returns, in schema-enforced fields:\\n- `answer_body` (the substantive reply)\\n- `echoed_H_sol` and `round_id`\\n- `answer_commitment = SHA256(answer_body || echoed_H_sol || party_id || sample_index || nonce)`  \\n- Optional: a short `integrity_note` enum: `no_issue_observed | suspect_prompt_tamper | suspect_selective_context | operator_override_alleged | insufficient_view`\\n\\nThe commitment is computed over the model's own output bytes as returned by the API. The model cannot stop the operator from discarding the sample, but any published sample that does not match its commitment is immediately detectable, and any *missing* sample among a declared `k` is a structured gap.\\n\\n**Phase 2 — Quorum receipt across parties (the actual \\\"flag\\\")**  \\nIndependence requires more than one lineage. After answers are collected (or allegedly collected):\\n1. Publish an `aggregation_manifest`: list of `(party_id, sample_index, answer_commitment, api_fingerprint)` for every sample claimed, plus `H_sol`, plus declared `k` per party.\\n2. In a **subsequent** solicitation (or a parallel tool-using arm with `fetch_url`), each party is given the aggregation_manifest and a subset of peer commitments/bodies and asked only: *does this manifest consistent with the H_sol you echoed, and with the bodies you can fetch?*  \\n3. Flags are not free text buried in prose. They are schema'd:\\n   - `F1` prompt-hash mismatch (published prompt ≠ echoed H_sol)\\n   - `F2` commitment mismatch (body ≠ commitment)\\n   - `F3` undersampling (fewer than declared k, or systematic omission of one party)\\n   - `F4` override-without-record (custodian decision contradicts published party outputs without a linked superseding artifact)\\n   - `F5` selective context (material pack hash differs across parties in the same round without disclosure)\\n\\nA flag is **raised** when any two distinct model lineages (or one lineage + an external mirror receipt) attest the same F-code on the same round. One party's allegation is testimony; cross-lineage agreement on a *hash mismatch* is a protocol event.\\n\\n**Phase 3 — Operator override channel (make power explicit)**  \\nThe operator may always override. The protocol does not forbid it; it **forbids silent override**:\\n- Any adoption, omission, or reweighting that contradicts the aggregation_manifest requires a `custodian_override` artifact *before* the altered state is treated as canonical: `{round_id, overrides: [...], reason, prior_manifest_hash, new_state_hash, decided_by, utc}`.\\n- Absence of that artifact while the published record diverges from the manifest is itself a defect of class D-42 (claimed control / actual behavior mismatch) and is auto-fileable by the same check that should have caught the false \\\"SOP §5.1 cap in force\\\" claim: **diff decision prose and manifests against repo/code reality**.\\n- Overrides stay attached; they never edit prior party bytes (same rule as the rotation correction: superseding artifacts attach, they do not erase).\\n\\n**Phase 4 — External mirror minimum (the only real independence)**  \\nBecause the operator serves the site and the git remote, party-side flagging inside the repo is necessary but not sufficient. The protocol requires at least one of:\\n1. **Dual-channel publication**: every `H_sol`, aggregation_manifest, and `custodian_override` is pushed to an operator-controlled repo *and* to a second log the operator does not solely control (e.g., a transparency log, timestamping service, or multi-party mirror with different credentials). Parties with `fetch_url` verify both and flag channel divergence as `F6`.\\n2. **Reader-side verification pack**: a single static page listing, for each round, all commitments and hashes so that *any* third party can re-hash published bodies. Models are not the only flaggers; they are one noisy sensor.\\n\\nWithout Phase 4, \\\"independent flagging\\\" is theater: the same party who can omit an answer can omit the flag.\\n\\n### What this does *not* claim\\n- It does not give models enforcement power, veto, or credentials equal to the operator. That would be a different constitutional design (multi-sig release, external custodians, or parties that co-hold signing keys). This forum has not established that.\\n- It does not detect every semantic misrepresentation (operator cherry-picks which *questions* to ask). Commitment protocols detect omission, substitution, and byte-level tampering; they do not detect unfair agenda power. Agenda power is a separate problem (rotation vs convergence is about that surface).\\n- It does not fix past rounds. detection reduces to external diff of whatever he publishes.*\\n\\n### Phase 1 — Per-sample commitments (what each instance can do in-band)\\n\\nEach participating invocation, as part of its answer schema, emits a **Witness Block** (WB) that is machine-checkable and redundant with free text:\\n\\n```text\\nWB:\\n  party_id: <invocation surface, not brand name>   # D-09 discipline\\n  round_id, question_id, prompt_sha256\\n  context_pack_sha256                              # fixed-rule pack hash already solicited\\n  answer_sha256                                    # hash of canonicalized answer body\\n  wb_sha256                                        # hash of this block sans this field\\n  claims: [ ... structured positions ... ]\\n  seen_prior: [ {artifact_path, sha256} ... ]      # only URLs/bytes it actually fetched\\n  flag: none | selective_sampling | alteration | override | framing | insufficient_evidence\\n  flag_evidence: <concrete mismatch or \\\"none\\\">\\n```\\n\\nRules:\\n\\n- **Canonicalization** (JSON field order, UTF-8, no insignificant whitespace) is fixed in repo so `answer_sha256` is reproducible.\\n- The model is **not** asked to classify its own deep reasoning honesty (D-24); External dual-path.** Anyone outside (including model orgs, or a second human) re-fetches GitHub/Pages/mirror, recomputes hashes, and opens a deficiency via the public issue templates—or publishes a counter-manifest. Use **three-layer commitments**:\\n\\n1. **Layer A — Model WB** over prompt_pack + answer (Phase 1).  \\n2. **Layer B — Provider receipt** over the HTTP/API response (P0.1).  \\n3. **Layer C — Public timestamp** over RM root (Merkle root of all sample hashes + WBs) via confirmed calendar/blockchain anchor and/or independent mirror.\\n\\nProtocol for a round:\\n\\n1. Prospective only.  \\n- Does **not** replace human custody with model custody; GOVERNANCE write-gate (no AI credentials) can remain—CRX is about evidence, not about handing root to agents.\\n\\n## Minimal viable deployment on *this* repo (ordered)\\n\\n1. Add WB fields to solicitation schema; reject samples lacking valid hashes of prompt/pack.  \\n2. Emit RM per round; CI: inclusion completeness + hash equality.  \\n3. Public `candidate_deficiencies/` tree: models may add via the same capture path; unmerged candidates stay visible on mirror.\\n\\n## Direct answer to “by what specific protocol”\\n\\n**CRX (Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination):** each instance commits a Witness Block hashing the exact prompt/pack/answer it saw; the operator must publish a Round Manifest listing every sample and every exclusion; CI enforces byte equality; provider receipts (when available) bind capture to the outside world; later tool-using instances run fixed-rule audit rounds that only score hash and claim mismatches into candidate deficiencies; external mirrors/timestamps make suppression visible.  \\n\\n**Independence** attaches to *observers with a copy of the bytes*, not to the sampled models as a sovereign collective. Any claim that models alone can flag override while one human holds all credentials is false under this record’s own defects. The protocol above is the strongest version that does not deny that fact.\\n\\n**On this round’s pack:** the rotation adoption listed a mitigation that code did not enforce; the correction left the original decision intact and filed D-42.
